Pathogens.intro: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease. There are four main types you need to know for GCSE Combined Science.

sections.title: Types of Pathogen
points: Bacteria — prokaryotic; produce toxins that damage tissues; treated with antibiotics
Viruses — not cells; replicate inside host cells, destroying them; no antibiotic treatment
Fungi — eukaryotic; some cause skin infections; treated with antifungals
Protists — eukaryotic; often spread by vectors (e.g. mosquitoes)

sections.title: How Pathogens Spread
points: Direct contact — touching infected person or surfaces
Droplet infection — coughing/sneezing (e.g. flu, COVID-19)
Contaminated water — drinking infected water (e.g. cholera)
Vectors — carried by another organism (e.g. mosquitoes spread malaria)

keyTerms.def: A microorganism that causes disease
An organism that carries and transmits a pathogen without getting the disease itself
A poisonous substance produced by bacteria that damages body cells

examTips: Viruses are NOT killed by antibiotics — antibiotics only work on bacteria.
Know the difference: bacteria produce toxins; viruses destroy host cells from the inside.
commonMistakes: Saying antibiotics kill viruses — they do not.

Viral Diseases.intro: Viruses cause disease by replicating inside host cells and destroying them. You need to know measles, HIV and tobacco mosaic virus.

sections.title: Measles
points: Symptoms: fever, red skin rash
Spread: droplet infection
Can be fatal if complications arise (e.g. brain damage)
Prevented by MMR vaccine

sections.title: HIV
points: HIV attacks the immune system (white blood cells)
Spread: sexual contact, sharing needles, mother to child
Can lead to AIDS — immune system so damaged it cannot fight infections
Treated with antiretroviral drugs (not cured)
Prevented by: condoms, not sharing needles, testing

sections.title: Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV)
points: Affects plants (especially tobacco, tomatoes)
Causes mosaic pattern on leaves — patches of discolouration
Chloroplasts disrupted — reduces photosynthesis
Spread by: contact between plants, contaminated tools

keyTerms.def: Human Immunodeficiency Virus — attacks white blood cells, weakening the immune system
Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome — late stage HIV where the immune system fails
Tobacco Mosaic Virus — a plant virus causing mosaic discolouration of leaves

examTips: HIV is treated but not cured — antiretroviral drugs prevent it developing into AIDS.
TMV reduces photosynthesis because it disrupts chloroplasts.
commonMistakes: Saying HIV can be cured — it cannot, only managed.
Forgetting TMV is a plant disease.

Bacterial Diseases.intro: Bacteria cause disease by producing toxins. You need to know salmonella and gonorrhoea for Combined Science.

sections.title: Salmonella
points: Causes food poisoning: fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea
Spread: contaminated food (undercooked poultry, eggs)
Bacteria produce toxins in the gut
Prevention: thorough cooking of food, hygiene, vaccination of poultry in UK

sections.title: Gonorrhoea
points: Sexually transmitted infection (STI)
Symptoms: thick yellow/green discharge, pain urinating. Some have no symptoms.
Treated with antibiotics (but antibiotic-resistant strains are increasing)
Prevention: condoms, testing and treating infected partners

keyTerms.def: Bacterium causing food poisoning through contaminated food
A sexually transmitted bacterial infection
When bacteria evolve so that antibiotics no longer kill them

examTips: Gonorrhoea is becoming harder to treat due to antibiotic-resistant strains — a key evaluative point.
Salmonella is prevented by vaccination of poultry in the UK.
commonMistakes: Confusing the symptoms of salmonella with food allergies.
Forgetting that some people with gonorrhoea have no symptoms.

Fungal and Protist Diseases.intro: Fungi and protists can also cause disease in plants and animals. Rose black spot and malaria are the key examples.

sections.title: Rose Black Spot (Fungal)
points: Caused by a fungus
Purple/black spots on leaves → leaves turn yellow and drop
Reduces photosynthesis and weakens plant
Spread: water, wind
Treatment: fungicides, removing and destroying infected leaves

sections.title: Malaria (Protist)
points: Caused by a protist (Plasmodium)
Symptoms: fever, sweating, shaking — can be fatal
Spread by female Anopheles mosquito (the vector)
Prevention: insect repellent, mosquito nets, anti-malarial drugs, draining stagnant water
No vaccine currently in widespread use

keyTerms.def: A disease caused by the protist Plasmodium, spread by mosquitoes
A fungal disease of roses causing black spots on leaves
The protist that causes malaria

examTips: The mosquito is the VECTOR for malaria — it carries the Plasmodium protist but is not itself the pathogen.
Rose black spot is prevented by fungicides AND removing infected leaves.
commonMistakes: Saying malaria is caused by mosquitoes — mosquitoes are the vector; the pathogen is the protist Plasmodium.
Confusing fungal (rose black spot) with viral or bacterial diseases.

Defence Systems.intro: The body has several lines of defence to prevent pathogens from entering and to destroy those that do get in.

sections.title: Physical Barriers
points: Skin — physical barrier preventing pathogen entry; sebum (oil) has antibacterial properties
Nose hairs and mucus — trap pathogens in airways; cilia move mucus up and out
Trachea and bronchi — lined with ciliated cells and mucus-secreting cells

sections.title: Chemical Defences
points: Stomach acid (HCl) — kills most pathogens in food and drink
Tears — contain lysozyme enzyme which destroys bacteria
Skin oils (sebum) — antibacterial properties

keyTerms.def: Sticky substance lining airways that traps pathogens and particles
Hair-like projections on cells that move mucus and trapped particles away from lungs
Enzyme found in tears and saliva that destroys bacterial cell walls

examTips: The skin is the FIRST line of defence. If pathogens get past it, the immune system responds.
Cilia move mucus away from the lungs — they are part of the physical defence, not the immune response.
commonMistakes: Confusing mucus (traps pathogens) with antibodies (destroy pathogens).
Forgetting that stomach acid kills most pathogens before they reach the gut.

Immune System.intro: When pathogens get past the body's physical defences, the immune system responds. White blood cells play a central role.

sections.title: Phagocytes
points: Engulf and digest pathogens — phagocytosis
Non-specific — attack any pathogen
Fast response

sections.title: Lymphocytes
points: Produce antibodies — specific to each pathogen's antigens
Antibodies bind to antigens on pathogens → clump them together → phagocytes destroy them
Also produce antitoxins to neutralise toxins
Memory cells remain — give immunity if same pathogen re-enters

sections.title: Antigens and Antibodies
sections.text: Antigens are proteins on the surface of pathogens. Each antibody is complementary to a specific antigen — like a lock and key.

callout.label: Key Point
callout.text: Antibodies are specific — one type of antibody only works against one specific antigen. Memory cells allow faster response to second infection.

keyTerms.def: White blood cell that engulfs and destroys pathogens
White blood cell that produces antibodies
A protein on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response
A protein produced by lymphocytes that binds to a specific antigen
Long-lived lymphocyte that enables rapid immune response upon second infection

examTips: Antibodies are complementary to antigens — use 'specific' or 'complementary' in exam answers.
Memory cells are the basis of immunity — they allow faster, larger response on second exposure.
Secondary immune response is faster and stronger than primary.
commonMistakes: Saying antibodies kill pathogens directly — they mark pathogens for destruction by phagocytes.
Confusing antigens (on pathogen) with antibodies (made by lymphocytes).

Vaccination.intro: Vaccines protect individuals and communities from infectious diseases by training the immune system to respond to specific pathogens.

sections.title: How Vaccines Work
numbered: A dead or weakened form of a pathogen (or its antigens) is injected
The immune system produces antibodies against the antigens
If the real pathogen enters later, memory cells produce antibodies rapidly before symptoms appear

sections.title: Herd Immunity
sections.text: If enough of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily — even unvaccinated people are protected. This is herd immunity.

callout.label: Evaluate
callout.text: Vaccines have side effects in some people, but the benefits (protection, herd immunity, eradication of disease) outweigh the risks in most cases.

keyTerms.def: A preparation containing dead/weakened pathogens or antigens that stimulates immunity
Protection of unvaccinated individuals because enough of the population is immune
Long-lived lymphocytes produced after vaccination or infection that enable rapid response

examTips: Vaccines contain antigens, not live dangerous pathogens (usually).
Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated (e.g. newborns, immunocompromised people).
commonMistakes: Saying vaccines contain the disease — they contain antigens or dead/weakened forms only.
Forgetting that vaccines work through memory cells, not direct antibodies.

Drugs.intro: Drugs are chemical substances that affect the way the body works. Understanding different types of drugs and how they work is required for B3.

sections.title: Painkillers
points: Relieve symptoms but do NOT kill pathogens
Examples: paracetamol, aspirin, ibuprofen
Aspirin was originally extracted from willow bark

sections.title: Antibiotics
points: Kill bacteria or prevent them reproducing
Do NOT work on viruses
Must be taken correctly to prevent antibiotic resistance
Penicillin — first antibiotic, discovered by Alexander Fleming

sections.title: Antibiotic Resistance
sections.text: Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics through natural selection:

callout.label: Critical Issue
callout.text: MRSA is an example of a 'superbug' — resistant to many antibiotics. To slow resistance: complete courses, don't use antibiotics unnecessarily, develop new antibiotics.

keyTerms.def: A drug that kills or prevents growth of bacteria — does not affect viruses
When bacteria evolve so that antibiotics no longer kill them
A drug that relieves pain without killing the pathogen
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — a bacterium resistant to many antibiotics

examTips: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only — never viral.
Completing antibiotic courses prevents resistance developing.
Painkillers treat symptoms; antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
commonMistakes: Saying antibiotics treat viral infections like the flu or COVID-19 — they do not.
Forgetting that resistance develops by natural selection (not bacteria 'trying' to survive).

Drug Development.intro: New drugs must go through extensive testing before they can be used. Understanding the process of drug development and clinical trials is required for B3.

sections.title: How New Drugs are Developed
numbered: Discovery — new drug identified (from plants, microorganisms, or designed by computer)
Pre-clinical testing — tested on cells, tissues, and animals to check safety and toxicity
Clinical trials — tested on human volunteers: small doses first, then larger groups

sections.title: Clinical Trials
points: Phase 1 — small group of healthy volunteers; checks for safety and side effects
Phase 2 — larger group of patients; checks for effectiveness and optimal dose
Phase 3 — large randomised controlled trial; double-blind trial (neither patient nor doctor knows who gets real drug)
Placebo — inactive substance given to control group to compare against real drug
Double-blind — prevents bias from patients or doctors

sections.title: Thalidomide
sections.text: Thalidomide was a drug developed as a sleeping pill but given to pregnant women for morning sickness. It caused limb abnormalities in thousands of babies. This led to much stricter drug testing protocols.

callout.label: Case Study
callout.text: Thalidomide is now used to treat leprosy and some cancers — showing that a drug can be harmful in one context but useful in another.

keyTerms.def: A test of a new drug on human volunteers to assess safety and effectiveness
An inactive substance given to the control group in a clinical trial
A trial where neither patients nor doctors know who receives the drug or placebo
Drug that caused birth defects when given to pregnant women; now used for leprosy/cancer

examTips: Double-blind trials prevent bias — if doctors knew who had the drug they might treat patients differently.
Placebos allow scientists to distinguish real drug effects from psychological effects.
Thalidomide is used as a case study for why drug testing must include effects on pregnancy.
commonMistakes: Confusing double-blind (both patient and doctor unaware) with single-blind (only patient unaware).
Saying placebos have no effect — they can have a psychological (placebo) effect.
